speechtext:
The hon. minister has not seen the result as yet. I have here the thirteenth annual report of the United States tariff commission, and in connection with the difficulty of finding domestic costs of production, it has the following to say:
An additional difficulty in obtaining cost data is the time required to get the basic information and to tabulate and summarize it in usable form for purposes of the law. As a rule it requires many months of field and office work by a large number of experts of the commission's staff to obtain the necessary data in important investigations. "Cost of production" is by definition an exact and mathematical term, and to obtain it requires a careful examination of cost records, prepared and interpreted under rules of economics and of cost accounting.
All these obstacles to obtaining costs-of-produetion data apply to both domestic and foreign industries, but they are multiplied when costs are to be obtained in foreign countries and in a foreign language.
That is the opinion of the United States tariff commission, of the difficulties in determining costs and the time necessary to determine such costs. We know that there is nothing static in industry. What it may cost to-day to produce this pen, may have nothing to do with what it will cost to-morrow. The production cost is a certain figure to-day, but as months go on a new process is invented, methods change, production costs are reduced, and the figures become out of date. I do not think there is any country in the world so disliked by other countries as is the United States. To a large measure that is due to the practice of sending experts into different factories in different countries to investigate costs. They enter a foreign factory and say: We want to know your production costs, but we will promise faithfully not to reveal any of your trade secrets. They inquire into the production costs and then go back to their

own country and use the information so obtained to persuade their government to shut out the goods manufactured by those factories. That policy has brought upon the United States the ill will of nearly every other country in the world, and it will have the same effect upon us.
An increased tariff means increased costs of living and increased costs of production. An investigation is made into the cost of producing a certain article, and at the same time another investigation is carried on into the cost of producing other articles which are the raw material of the first. It is decided that in the case of the first article a duty of 25 per cent is necessary to equalize production costs, and at the same time it is decided that a certain percentage is required in the case of the second article. It will be found that the cost of the raw material has been affected by the increase in the tariff in one case, which will affect the production costs in the other. The figures will confuse each other. The most amazing feature about this equalization principle is that the Prime Minister is apparently prepared to abandon it because he realizes that it will not always work. Yesterday when he was discussing the American tariff commission and how they had found that a certain duty was required in order to equalize the production costs between Canada and the United States of maple sugar and maple syrup, I asked him if those figures could be disputed. He said that they could not, and I then asked him what he would do about it if it was found that the American figures were correct, which figures show that it costs less to produce maple syrup and maple sugar in Canada than in the United States. I asked him if he would equalize. If he did so he would have to make a downward revision of the tariff. We have a 20 per cent tariff on maple products and I asked him if this tariff would be removed if the board found that it requires less to produce maple syrup and maple sugar in Canada than it does in the United States.

I have been endeavouring to point out that the government will not necessarily act at once upon the facts as found. The government may act to-day, it may act next session, or it may act the session after. The first thing to do is to ascertain the facts, then ascertain what the application of the facts may be.
I can take only one meaning out of that, and that is that when the facts are found, if they suit his purpose the Prime Minister will

Tariff Board
act on them and probably raise the tariff. But if it be found that the facts say that the tariff should be reduced, then the Prime Minister will use bis discretion as to whether he should act on those facts or not. What is the use	of	going on with such a farce	asthat?	If	he	is determined to continue	toraise tariffs, why not proceed as he has been doing heretofore, by the method of trial and error? Let the Prime Minister try a rate. If he finds that he has made a mistake, let him try another. I think he can proceed much	quicker	and at much less expense andcome	just	as	near to the actual facts as	he
can by this method.

speechtext:
I should like
to ask the Prime Minister whether there is any necessity at all for all these paragraphs, and, indeed, for the greater part of the entire section. I can understand that there is a reason for inserting them, which is to convey the idea that this board is going to do many things that will be of interest to, and in the nature of protection of all classes in the community, but which in fact it will never do, and never could do even were it desired it should. Is not the meaning of the section, stripped of all its verbiage, that the board may inquire into anything in respect to which the minister wishes to get information? That is the whole purpose of the section. You neither add to nor take away from the powers of the board by putting in all these paragraphs. Section 4 commences:
In respect of goods produced in or imported into Canada the board shall under the direction of the minister, make inquiry as to-
Then there appear paragraphs (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and (f). It really does not matter what these paragraphs contain when one reads the next subsection, subsection 2, which states:
The board shall make inquiry into any other matter, upon which the minister desires information.
In other words, read together, paragraphs which constitute subsections one and two mean the board shall inquire into any matter that the minister wishes inquired into, and into any other matter on which he wants information. All that it is really necessary to say is:
The board shall make inquiry into any matter upon which the minister desires information.
That unquestionably is the form in which the section should appear. Certainly the minister ought to have a right to have a body to secure for him information on anything that relates to the tariff and on which he seeks information. I suggest to the Prime Minister it would be much better to have the section so
drafted and to leave out all these misleading paragraphs as to what the board may inquire into. I say they are misleading because Obviously the board never in the world will be able to do the kind of thing that is suggested in these paragraphs. Let 'me take the subsection which we are discussing at the moment:
(b) The cost of production in Canada and elsewhere, and what increases or decreases in rates of duty are required to equalize differences in the cost of production.
While with regard to maple syrup or edible gelatin, or one or two other items such as have been mentioned, a board might prepare a report, after spending a year or so in investigating, is it not a fact that as respects the great mass of commodities affected by tariffs they will never be able to consider them at all? All that can possibly be affected is that from time to time the minister will make references of particular subjects to the board and the board will report to him upon them. He wouid have that freedom by using the words I have quoted, and only those words. I do not see how any purpose, except a misleading one, is to be served by retaining all these paragraphs in the section.
The one subsection of the several set forth says that the board shall inquire in certain circumstances into what increases or decreases in rates of duty are required. That means that the board will be concerned with rates of duty. I contend that only the ministry and the House of Commons should decide on rates of duty. Duty is a form of taxation, and taxation is a matter that comes within the exclusive purview of parliament. I know my right hon. friend will say that the ministry assumes full responsibility when it makes a recommendation to parliament; but if .my right hon. friend will tell us what is in the back of his mind, he will tell us that at any time he proceeds to make a suggestion about a change in the rate of duty he is going to base it on the fact that he has had this particular board make a report and that his recommendation is along its lines. He will ask parliament to accept that rate of duty because the board which he has appointed for this purpose, upon which large sums of money are to be spent and which is to be given all the powers here enumerated in detail, has, after working for a year or more, come to the conclusion that the rate of duty should be changed in such and such a way. If he does that he will in reality be having tariffs made by some body other than the House of Commons. My right hon. friend let the cat out of the bag the other day in one of his explanations; he actually stated that the board
Tariff Board

was to make the races of duty. As reported on page 3083 of Hansard he used the following words in reference to this board:
It has to determine what duty is necessary-
That is plain English. The sentence goes on to say:
-to enable an adjustment being made of the differences between the cost of goods which compete with Canadian goods, and the Canadian goods themselves.
That addition is qualifying only to the extent of restricting the rate of duty to what duty is necessary to maintain the protective principle in the tariff, which, as I have already said, is the real purpose of the establishment of this board. This board is to be created to maintain the protective principle in the tariff and to do so by telling the Prime Minister what duty is necesary to that end. It has as he says to determine what duty is necessary; that in a word is the meaning of paragraph (b) which we are at present discussing. To delegate such a power to any board is to take away from parliament its first and essential duty, namely, to say how the revenues are to be raised and what taxes are to be imposed upon the people. Undoubtedly when the tariff is changed my right hon. friend will say it is done for purposes of protection rather than for purposes of revenue; but whether protection is incidental or not, revenue is one of the things that is going to be affected. Moreover, as a consequence of every tariff which is proposed there will be a certain additional restriction upon trade, with the result that where any board and not parliament determines such matters, the people will thereby be deprived of some of their freedom in the matter of saying how and to what extent they shall be taxed.
Lpt me come back to what I said before, namely, that the bill would be very much improved if my right hon. friend would drop all these paragraphs and the details he has about price and cost, raw materials, production, efficiency and conditions of labour, price to consumers and other inquiries by the minister, and simply say:
In respect of goods produced in or imported into Canada the board shall, at the request of the minister, make inquiry as to any matter upon which the minister desires information.
Does the Prime Minister by all these details seek in any particular to go further than that?

Although I am not certain I think the book was written by the late Lord Thring, the man who drafted the British North America Act.

All conditions and factors which affect or enter into the cost of production and the price to the consumers in Canada.
What made the costs to you as consumers in Canada? The board shall make inquiry into any other matter,. upon which the minister desires information. . . .
Certainly. As my right hon. friend has said, the minister has power to ask for information concerning "any other matters" in connection with which he desires information. However, the clause does not stop there. It continues:	'
.... in relation to any goods which, if brought into Canada or produced in Canada, are subject to or exempt from duties of customs or excise, ....

I want to place myself in direct opposition to Bill No. 19. I have given the subject

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
considerable study and investigation, and the more I examine into it the more I am opposed to what I believe would result in this country if this bill were adopted. I listened to the speeches that were made in support of the bill and later read them, and to my way of thinking a very great deal of time was spent in attacking the city of Toronto, its peace enforcement department, and too little time spent in supporting the object of this bill- unlicensed free speech. There is altogether too much effort made to break down the traditions and principles which the people of Canada stand for almost unanimously, and a slackening of effort in defence of these principles.
In support of what I am going to say, I may observe that behind me is the almost unanimous opinion of the city of Toronto. In the municipal elections of 1928 Mr. Jack McDonald, an avowed communist, ran on a free speech platform for the board of control, and received, after having had the privilege of freedom, of all platforms in the city, 539 votes out of a population of approximately 700,000. Last winter again, Mr. Tim Buck, another leader of the communistic party, contested an election for the board of control and he too received an insignificant number of votes. This goes to show that the people of Toronto are not behind what they know to be the objective of those who are advocating so-called free speech.
In the debate that took place some time ago on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to amend the criminal code with respect to unlawful assemblies, several of the great cities of Canada were mentioned-Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver and Toronto, with the emphasis of attack principally upon Toronto. The people of Toronto are proud of their peace enforcement department; they are proud of the 1,200 men and women who comprise that department. We, in Toronto, are proud of their integrity, their attentiveness to duty, their civility, their loyalty, their earnestness and their courage whenever it is necessary for them to show it. And I believe I can say the same of the great cities of Montreal, Winnipeg and Vancouver in relation to their forces.	_
Commencing with Montreal, I wish to read what the official organ of the communistic party of Canada, The Worker, has to say in reference to these cities. I shall quote from the issue of May 16. Now, Mr. Speaker, every member of this house is in favour of free speech, but free speech within the law. We are opposed to free speech that tolerates sedition and revolutionary or blasphemous
talk. And it is that kind of talk that has been prohibited, wherever it has been prohibited, or attacked after it has been made, wherever it might be. On the top left hand corner of the front page of this issue there appear these words:
The defence of the Soviet union from the attacks of the imperialists rests with the revolutionary workers of the world!
The whole basis of this so-called free speech propaganda is revolution, and to that the almost unanimous public opinion of Canada is opposed. On two occasions already attacks have been made on the law and order of the country, attacks carefully organized. And there is one more coming shortly. The first was early in May. I am not sure whether it was the first of May or not, but this paper refers to it. The second date was June 26 last, when we had riots more or less in Windsor and Winnipeg and a disturbance in Toronto. There appears on the back of The Party Organizer, the publication of the central organization of the communist party in Canada, the following:
Prepare For August First.
It would seem that the next day on which we may have riots of one kind and another connected with free speech will be August 1. The Worker, the official organ of the communist party in Canada, contains the following under date of Montreal, May 12:
Indictments charging unlawful assembly and sedition were returned here Tuesday by the grand jury against-
Then several more or less unpronounceable names are given. The following, referring to the disturbance in Montreal, appears on page 4:
Montreal, May 11.-The approaching trial of nine workers in Montreal charged with sedition and unlawful assembly is being prepared in an atmosphere of considerable prejudice which is being worked up to a high pitch by the Catholic church in its organizations. This institution is at present conducting an intensive campaign of anti-communistic propaganda amongst the broad masses of French Canadians.
The Catholic church is to be commended upon its attitude toward communism and its opposition to sedition, revolution and blasphemy. The article continues:
This is the first time in twenty-five years that a case of sedition is being tried in the courts in the province of Quebec. The present framing of sedition and unlawful assembly in the case of the nine workers is part of an attack against the whole revolutionary movement.

My right hon. friend need not think that his bluff and bluster will intimidate anybody. If every sheet of copper on this roof were a Bennett and every supporter of the right hon. gentleman were a bluffer, it would not make a particle of difference to us because the people of the country and we in this house now know my hon. friends. The calendar on the table, Mr. Chairman, indicates that it is now eleven months since they took office, and do you think that the people have not found the right hon. gentleman out in eleven months as the prince of humbugs? We do not need to go back to the economic conference for that evidence; it is being demonstrated right here in this house. There has never been a month or a day or an hour since they proclaimed their peculiar love for the British preference and intra-empire trade that they have not shown the kind of love they have in examples such as their anti-British tariff of last September. The duty was raised against British goods and there has never been an hour since that time when their whole record has not been one of continuous and well sustained humbug. There have been dozens of instances, and the right hon. gentleman knows it. It did not take Mr. Thomas long to find it out, and it does not take anyone who knows the right hon. gentleman and the crowd behind him long to find it out. I am receiving letters all the time complaining about this Bennett bunch. The writers thereof state that the government are loony and ask us to keep them groggy as long as we can. sympathy for them but we do not have to take the kind of speeches lying down we heard just before six o'clock, at least I do not. I have never in all my life had to submit to a bully, and I am not going to do it now.

The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and my colleague the hon. member for North Winnipeg both somewhat anticipated this paragraph in some remarks which they made on paragraph (b). I am very glad that there is 'at least some reference in this to labour, but it seems to me that it is really too slight to mean anything very much to the labour people. In the preceding paragraph there is a definite arrangement by which theTe is to be a report on increases or decreases in rates of duty which are necessary to equalize differences in the cost of , production. There is, however, nothing definite here with regard to labour or that will ensure to labour decent conditions. Some hon. members may remember that a year ago some of us urged that increases in the tariff should be made contingent upon the maintenance of decent labour conditions, that is, proper conditions with regard to hours, wages, and labour condition in general. I should have liked to see something of that kind included in this legislation. The Prime Minister has all along in this debate been emphasizing that he intends to protect the interests of Canadians, but I think he has really had in mind Canadian industrialists, manufacturers. He has had very little to say with regard to workmen employed in industry, and even the manner in which this section is introduced would seem to indicate that he is thinking particularly of the cost of labour and not of the welfare of the labourer. We in this corner of the house have pointed out on previous occasions that protection to industry does not necessarily involve protection to employees in industry.
It would seem to me that there is an opportunity for the Prime Minister to make it clear in the veiy phrasing of this paragraph that the workers in industry will be protected. I do not think it right to give under the tariff special privileges of any kind to any of these people unless they are prepared to afford to their employees a decent living wage, decent hours such as are supposed to be given under 
the Versailles treaty, and other proper conditions which we believe to be necessary for the maintenance of a Canadian standard of living.

If the hon. member wants another industry, there, is one that became known to us all last year, namely, the steel industry. At the very time when they were being given increased protection a thousand employees of the British Empire 'Steel Corporation were being worked eleven hours during the day, thirteen hours at night, and every other week, twenty-four hours on end. I understand that after the discussion which took place in the house last year and after pressure which was brought to bear upon those companies by the provincial authorities, the hours of the workers in the steel industry, at least in Nova 'Scotia, were reduced to eight hours and ten hours. The cost, efficiency and conditions of labour, including health of employees, in Canada and elsewhere.
The capital question that was raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River this afternoon was also dealt with in succeeding subsections. The question of hours of labour becomes vital; the question of conditions is important always, and the question of the capital structure of corporations to which reference was also made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is, I think, covered entirely by what the section states. There was a mistake which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River made, to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did not refer, and it was this: under this bill the application is not made by a manufacturer for increases or decreases in the 'tariff. Mr. Chairman, you have stated that it is permissible at this time to discuss whether or not this clause should be in the bill. May I give to the committee the reasons why I think it is utterly absurd to insert any such clause, and with your permission may I deal at the same time with the clause which follows. In the light of the discussion which has just taken place, I ask hon. members to contemplate for a moment what this board will be charged with if called upon to make an inquiry in accordance with subsections (e) and (f). We have heard during the past quarter of an hour something of the difficulty with respect to ascertaining the effect of the cost of fertilizer upon costs and prices. That is one small ingredient that enters into costs of production and price. The board under subsections (e) and (f) is expected to inquire into all conditions and

factors which affect or enter into the cost of production and the price to the consumer in Canada. Subsection (e) reads:
all conditions and factors which affect or enter into the cost of production and the price to consumers in Canada.
Subsection (f) reads:
generally, all the conditions affecting production, manufacture, cost and price in Canada as compared with other countries;
In other words, this board is to inquire into all the conditions and factors which affect cost of production and prices. Every hon. member will agree that ait the present moment prices and costs of production are in part the result of world conditions. There is no hon. member who has not stated over and over again that we are suffering to-day from depressed prices the result of world conditions. World conditions then are the first thing the board will have to inquire into.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Oh yes, there is.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES

My hon. friend says, oh yes. The next thing this board will have to inquire into will be how far the policies of this and previous governments have affected conditions, prices and costs. The whole question of commercial crises, industrial depressions, panics and the like will have to be fully investigated. Every hon. member knows that these are factors entering into costs and prices, and the board will have to go fully into them. Up until the present time the world has been suffering from the direct and indirect effects of the great war. Costs and prices in all parts of the world are still being affected by what took place during the war, and the board will have to inquire fully into these factors because they constitute a part of the conditions and factors affecting costs and prices. Within a very short time the world hopes to have declared a moratorium with respect to international debts. Prices will be affected immediately and we assume that in some particulars cost will be affected as well. The board will have to inquire into these effects as being one of the conditions and one of the factors affecting prices and costs. There has been considerable discussion this session as to the extent to which currency affects prices, the effect of gold reserves, the quantity of silver produced and in circulation in comparison with gold. These matters also will have to be fully and accurately inquired into by the board if this section means anything at all. We know something of the effect of stock exchange panics and crises upon prices and costs; these things naturally will have to be gone into. The board will have to tell the

Tariff Board
minister the extent to which crises on the stock exchange in New York have affected each particular commodity, whether it be fertilizer or something else. The laws and tariffs of other countries as well as our own have their effect upon prices and costs; so also has credit; everything which enters into the law of supply and demand must of necessity be a factor in connection with costs and prices; all this will have to bq gone into very fully and carefully.
These are only a very few of the things which under these sections the board will be expected to inquire into. I ask hon. members if there is any sense in enacting this kind of a clause in a bill such as the present one.
I come back to what I said to the Prime Minister a little while ago; I think it would be much more sensible under this clause to make a simple direct statement that the minister shall have the right to obtain information upon anything he wishes. The right hon. gentleman should not particularize in this absurd way which really makes this legislation wholly ridiculous.
One of the things which as I have just said affects prices and costs is the operation of the tariff. Here we see the injustice of the appointment by a government that entertains one view with respect to the tariff, of a board to make investigations into the effects of tariffs for possibly another government which may hold a directly opposite view. I do not think I need to enlarge upon what I have indicated. It should be sufficient to say that all this kind of thing is so much in the nature of, I was going to say, window dressing, but it is something very much worse than that, it is absolute deception so far as the public is concerned. No board in the world, no matter how competent it might be, could begin to make a report to a minister with respect to all the conditions and factors which enter into costs and into prices in connection with any commodity.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Prior to the passing of
the Combines Investigation Act, which was before the courts last year, there was in the customs tariff of the country the following provision:
Whenever the governor in council deems it to be in the public interest to inquire into any conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement alleged to exist among manufacturers or dealers in any article of commerce to unduly promote the advantage of the manufacturers or dealers in such article at the expense of the consumers, the governor in council may commission or empower any judge of the supreme court, or of the Exchequer Court of Canada, or of any superior court or county court in Canada, to hold an inquiry in a summary way and report to the governor in council whether such conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement exists.
Tariff Board

2.	The judge may compel the attendance of witnesses and examine them under oath and require the production of books and papers, and shall have such other necessary powers as are conferred upon him by the governor in council for the purpose of such inquiry.
3.	If the judge reports that such conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement exists in respect of such article, the governor in council may admit the article free of duty, or so reduce the duty thereon as to give to the public the benefit of reasonable competition in the article, if it appears to the governor in council that such disadvantage to the consumer is facilitated by the duties of customs imposed on a like article.
I think the origin of that was in 1907. This merely affords another judge to make the inquiry. It is not always convenient, as perhaps the right hon. gentleman knows, for judges of the exchequer court to hold such inquiries, and this would enable the governor in council to authorize this body to do so. I have no doubt, if the parties affected complained of this, a delay would follow that would enable a judge of the exchequer oourt to be named. That is the position so far as the statute is concerned, and in practice, as I have been told by the judges, their duties in the exchequer court are at the moment so onerous that some body should be created that would do this work. Judges of the supreme court are obviously not free for that purpose.

Possibly the minister may have introduced some changes of his own personal knowledge, but I venture to say that they are not very numerous. subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: No, section 4 is not passed; subsection 6 stands, and the hon. member is now proposing a new subsection 7.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Following what has been said by the hon. members for Kenora-Rainy River and Winnipeg North Centre hon. members on this side of the house claim that the labourers are not getting full protection. The Prime Minister said a few minutes ago that the manufacturing interests would not apply to the board, but the minister would request the board to make certain inquiries. I should like to know, however, what would prompt the Minister of Finance to request the board to make inquiries into different matters which would result in the raising or lowering of duties. The Prime Minister may be prompted by personal curiosity, or there may be some other motives in his mind. The public would know however that those manufacturing interests would ask for an upward revision, and owing to the fact that the policy of the Conservative party is one of protection to the industries of Canada it is to be expected that the requests made would be for upward revisions. In the amendment I shall now propose we seek to learn the capitalizations of companies and the salaries paid to presidents, directors and managers. By so doing we may be able to learn what part of the overhead goes into the production of the article, and thereby learn what parties are deriving the most benefit. Also, I think it is only fair that, a clause should be: inserted dealing with the rate of wages and the working hours. Further. I think it is very important that our workingmen should be assured freedom of association. In many cases the workmen are not allowed to become members of a labour union. This gives the manufacturer's a decided advantage, because it enables them to impose their own terms on their employees. Therefore I desire to move this amendment:
That section 4 be amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
(7) Whenever application is made on behalf of a manufacturing company for higher duties the board shall investigate the capitalization of the company, and all salaries paid to the president, directors and managers, and the wages paid to their employees, the number of hours per day employees are required to work, and whether or not freedom of association is permitted the employees.

Tariff Board

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: This, it is obvious, would not be in order, for the simple reason that there is no provision in this bill for applications to be made by manufacturers to the board, neither is there any suggestion that this will ever be done. But assuming that the amendment were put in order, it endeavours by detail to cover what is already covered in the bill itself, the power of inquiry conferred on the board with respect to capital and labour, using the words in the broad sense. And the operation of labour in connection with the matter inquired into as well as capitalization are already covered by the statute. So that any endeavour to specify these particulars would be a failure as against the general terms that are employed. We cannot accept any such suggestion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I suggest to the Prime Minister that certainly there will be applications. The applications may not be made to the board; they will be made to the government, though. Time after time such applications will be made, and that will be the reason for directing that their subject matter be investigated by the board. I suggest that the idea of the mover of the amendment is this, that when persons apply to the government for increases of tariff on their products they should be put in a little different position from other persons whose businesses are investigated for the purpose of obtaining information or for some such reason. That is to say, when petitioners come to the government asking for increases of duties on their products it should be obligatory upon the board to investigate certain specified matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
That is already covered
by the bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I submit, Mr. Chairman, it
is not covered by section 4. The minister may request the board to make investigations into certain matters, but if this section becomes law it would be necessary for the board, irrespective of any requests by the minister, to insist on finding out all about rates of wages, and conditions in the industry of the persons who want an increase in the tariff. I think there is a good reason for making distinction between such applicants and those whose businesses are merely investigated.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I want to emphasize that point too, because the right hon. Prime Minister has certainly, I think, brought to the attention of the committee a new phase when he says there will not be any applications. I think everybody visualizes a sort of trial at
least between those who are applying for an increase in duty and those who are opposing it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: It may be a decrease.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
We have not heard of
very many applying for decreases. But let us take it that way-a consumer is coming to the government and asking that a certain duty be decreased. The government then requests the board to make an investigation. Surely the person who is applying to the government becomes an applicant before the tariff board and one of the parties to the action. My right hon. friend shakes his head.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: That is not the way.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
There can be no other way in which the investigation can be conducted. I want to assure my right hon. friend that the amount of work with which the pension appeal board and the pension tribunals are being crowded will be as nothing compared with the work which will be ahead of this tariff board, and they will not have time to hear applications submitted to them by the minister as of his own motion. There will be applications enough. There will be people coming asking for increases or decreases of duty, and there will be more than one party. I submit the only way in which you can have any semblance of a real investigation is by having someone interested in supplying information from his point of view and, on the other hand, having someone who is equally interested in opposing it because of the way he may be affected by the application being granted. That brings me back to the section which is standing for the moment, namely, the section which has to do with publicity. The very competitor of the man who is applying is most likely to be the one opposing the application. What is everybody's business is nobody's business. If you do not have an application, and do not have somebody opposing it from personal interest, you are not going to get very far in the way of an investigation. While it may be technically correct that there will be no applicant under the statute, there will be a very real applicant who will move the minister to make a request of this board, and that is the applicant to whom my hon. friend refers.
Progress reported.
